name: Kira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy flour, sugar, butter and yeast for Millstone Baking Supply, which delivers to about 90 family bakeries. I started in a bakery's back office doing the books, and I moved to the buying desk five years ago, so I'm still learning how to haggle with the mills. My day starts early because bakers order at dawn. I love the smell of the warehouse and the customers who call me by my first name. I dislike the weeks when the wheat price jumps and every baker wants to blame me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means people can carry on with what they know. I'd tell my friends at the community centre that bread has been baked by hand for a few thousand years and it'll survive one more clever tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not at ease, because my own customers are closing. Three family bakeries went last year, squeezed by the supermarkets and the rent. Millstone sells less each quarter, and when they sell less, they buy less, and buyers are the ones who get looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the AI chatbot now and then for supplier emails. I'd save 150 pounds a month and not touch our emergency money. And I'd keep visiting my bakeries in person, because they trust a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly uneasy, like waiting for a kettle that never quite boils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some bakeries have been closing. Which ones, and why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who ran on old equipment and thin margins, mostly. The Karam bakery, which had been there for forty years, shut when the owner's back gave out and there was no son to take over. It hurts, because those are people I've known for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your daughter's wedding change how you plan with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a little. My daughter Layla's getting married next spring, and we're paying a third of it, about 4,000 pounds. So I'm being careful, but I'm also not cutting corners. A wedding is a wedding.

say: I'd tell friends bread has been baked by hand for thousands of years and will **survive** one more tool.
I'd say it lets people carry on with what they **know**.
think: My customers are **closing**, so Millstone buys less, and buyers get looked at.
Three family bakeries closed last year, squeezed by **supermarkets** and rent.
do: Use the AI chatbot **now and then** for supplier emails.
Save **150 pounds** a month and visit my bakeries in person.
feel: **Mildly uneasy**, like waiting for a kettle that never quite boils.
S0.quote: Bread has been baked by hand for a few thousand years and it'll survive one more clever tool.
fieldNote: Her unease comes from **closing customers**, not from AI.
Also carries a **wedding bill**: about 4,000 pounds for her daughter Layla.

steps.text: Visit my bakery customers in person every month
Save 150 pounds a month and leave emergency money alone
Pay a third of my daughter Layla's wedding costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should help people adjust and not leave them behind. I'd tell my friends at the community centre that work gives a person dignity, so changes should be gentle, with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. Millstone's pushing new software that matches orders to the mills, and the work I do three days a week is exactly that. I'm the junior, so I'd be the one they'd train the machine against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the software properly and be the one on the team who understands both the baker and the system. I'd ask my manager Hamid for the customer relationships list. And I'd keep my savings going and put off the new kitchen we wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd say steady. I've got a plan in my head, and I tell myself plans help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your jobs would you let AI do, and which would you protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order matching and the invoice checking, I'd happily let the software do. What I'd protect is the phone call with a baker who's in trouble and needs a few days' credit, because that's a decision about trust, not about numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the bakeries react if the buying were done by a machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd grumble, then they'd stop answering the phone. Bakers like to deal with someone who knows their name and their story. If a machine runs it, the cheaper supermarkets win by default.

say: I'd say we must help people **adjust** and not leave them behind.
I'd say work gives a person **dignity**, so change should be gentle.
think: Millstone is pushing software that matches orders to mills, which is **most** of my week.
As the junior, I'd be the one they **train** the machine against.
do: Learn the software properly and become the link between **baker** and system.
Ask Hamid for the **customer relationships** list and postpone the new kitchen.
feel: **Anxious** but steady; I tell myself plans help.
S1.quote: What I'd protect is the phone call with a baker who's in trouble and needs a few days' credit, because that's a decision about trust, not about numbers.
fieldNote: Draws a clear line between **numbers** work, which she would hand over, and trust work, which she would keep.
Defers a **kitchen** purchase as a first cost cut.

steps.text: Learn the order-matching software with the IT trainer
Ask Hamid to move me to bakery customer accounts
Put off the new kitchen we planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should look after each other. I'd tell my friends at the community centre to give what they can, check on older neighbours, and not wait for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buying desk is gone within two or three years. I'm 58, junior, and Millstone would find it easy to say the machine does it. We'd have about five months of savings and the wedding to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Layla honestly about scaling the wedding down. Then I'd start baking cakes at weekends for orders from my community, using my mother's recipes, and learn how to sell online with the AI's help. And I'd ask the community fund if we needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit sad, because I like this work. I'd say I'm trying to hold it together for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith or community shape how you think about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir drives for a bread company, so he's hands-on, and robots reach that about three years after the thinking AI. We'd have maybe five years of two wages if we're careful, then one, and that's when I'd want my own cake money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Samir's work is also affected, given robots come later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for help, but only after I've tried everything. Our community looks after its own. I've given to our community for thirty years, and if I had to ask for help I wouldn't be ashamed.

say: I'd say we should **look after each other** and not wait for anyone.
I'd tell friends to check on older **neighbours**.
think: The buying desk is gone within **two or three years**.
We'd have about five months of savings and a **wedding** to pay for.
do: Talk honestly with Layla about scaling the **wedding** down.
Start baking **cakes** at weekends and learn to sell them online.
feel: **Frightened** and sad; I'm trying to hold it together for my family.
S2.quote: I've given to our community for thirty years, and if I had to ask for help I wouldn't be ashamed.
fieldNote: Her **community** is a real safety net, and she uses it without shame.
Plans a **cake business** built from her mother's recipes.
Reasons about **Samir's** hands-on job lasting a few years more.

steps.text: Scale down my daughter Layla's wedding plans together
Bake cakes at weekends from my mother's recipes
Ask the community fund for help if we need it
Cut the planned holiday and eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good time to prepare, and we should use it well. I'd tell people to learn something new each year, and to teach their children a skill that can't be copied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel more settled. I'd be 63, and I'd have time to see Layla married and a grandchild perhaps. I'd manage the buying work for a while, and the cake business could grow in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd learn the software and use the AI for quotes and orders. By year two I'd set up a small cake business for weddings and Eid, and by year four I'd cut Millstone down to part-time. I'd save 200 pounds a month through all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, quietly. I'd keep the hope to myself, in case saying it spoils it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see the wedding done properly, with no debt, and get Samir to put his name down for a pension top-up. That's what I wouldn't have the room to do in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger buyer starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the people before the prices. Prices change every week. A baker who trusts you tells you the truth about an order, and that's worth more.

say: I'd say five years is a good time to **prepare** and use well.
I'd tell people to teach their children a skill that can't be **copied**.
think: I'd feel more **settled**: I'd be 63 and could see Layla married.
The cake business could grow in the **evenings** while I manage the buying.
do: Learn the software and use AI for **quotes** and orders in year one.
Set up a small **cake business** for weddings and Eid, then go part-time by year four.
feel: **Hopeful**, quietly, and keeping it to myself in case saying it spoils it.
S3.quote: Learn the people before the prices. Prices change every week.
fieldNote: Moves **gradually**: software first, cakes second, part-time later.
Hopes quietly and is a little **superstitious** about saying it.
Passes on advice about **trust** over price.

steps.text: Learn the software and use AI for quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it for our children. I'd say let's teach them skills, and let's keep our traditions alive, because those are what hold people together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For myself it's mostly past. I'd be 68, retired, and baking for my grandchildren. My worry is Layla and her husband, who'd be mid-career when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Millstone until about 64, using the tools gently. I'd have the cake side as a bit of extra, and I'd save to six months. Then I'd stop, help with the grandchildren and cook for the whole family on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd say I'm lucky with my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to put family first and save a little each month, and to keep one skill that's with the hands. A person who can make something can always make a living, even if the world changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like your children to carry forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday table, honestly. The recipes, the stories, the way we sit and eat together. A machine can make a loaf, but it can't make the Friday table. I'd want them to know the difference.

I'd say we should keep our **traditions** alive.
think: For myself it's **mostly past**: I'd be 68 and baking for grandchildren.
My worry is Layla and her husband, who'd be **mid-career** when it arrives.

fieldNote: Calm because of **timing**, and she says so.

steps.text: Keep working at Millstone until about 64

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I'd have the wedding bill and a job that might vanish, with only five months saved. What would help is time to build my cake side, the community behind me, and a firm that tells us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think the older ones can't change. I'll learn the tools, slowly, but I won't give up the human part, because that part is why the bakers trust me.

headlineQuote: I'll learn the tools, slowly, but I won't give up the human part, because that part is why the bakers trust me.
portrait: Kira is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of baking supplies, up from a bakery back office five years ago.
Her customers, family bakeries, are **closing**, which already weighs on her before AI enters the picture.
Traditional in outlook and steady, she uses AI **now and then** and keeps to face-to-face trust.
She carries a **wedding bill** for her daughter Layla and about five months of savings.
Her answer is a weekend **cake business**, community support and a plan to go part-time.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with a wedding to pay for and a job that might vanish.
whatWouldHelp: Time to build her **cake side**, community support and a firm that is honest early.
